turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, love, we'll get the checks done before the doctor. Blood pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that too low? I, umm, I keep thinking I'm going to collapse if it drops.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's a grand reading, honestly. Pulse is seventy-six. Temperature thirty-eight point three. Weight, uh, sixty-two... no, fifty-two kilograms, I was on the wrong line.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Right.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): For the pulse, last time in March you were sixty-eight. Your last pressure was one-forty. Those are the old ones, not today.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was going on about that one-forty the whole way in the car. I told her it was ancient.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Dr Brennan. Sit wherever you're comfortable. What's been happening?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the spinning, doctor. I'm really frightened. It only lasts a few seconds but I think I'm going to fall.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me in your own time how it comes on.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Since last week. Umm, if I turn over in the bed the room goes round. Same if I look up at the high press. Then it just stops.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She woke me in the night with it. Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday, I wouldn't swear.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): And I feel sick with it. Queasy in the stomach. I'm terrified it's something terrible.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): When the room spins, is there any pain with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it's not painful. It's the fright more than anything.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any ringing in the ears?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): And pain in the ear itself?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not that either.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Has the hearing dropped off at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I hear grand.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): The nurse had your blood pressure there. How long have you had the high blood pressure?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Years, I'd say. Was it last winter, or the one before? I couldn't put a date on it, err, it all blurs.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't look at me. She bins the letters. I haven't a clue of the year.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): And what are you taking for it at the minute?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodopine. Five milligrams, every morning. The small white one.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Did you stop any of the others along the way, or was there one you never actually started?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped the bendrofluazide in March. It had me up half the night to the toilet. And the chemist said a statin, atorvastin or something, but I never took that. Not once.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): With the blood pressure, do you get headaches?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I'm late with the tablet.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): And chest pain, or a tightness across the chest?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not the chest.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): When it spins, any weakness down an arm or a leg, double vision, or the words not coming out right?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I was certain it was a stroke though. Are you sure it isn't?
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): I hear you, those are exactly the things to check. We'll pin it down. Have you actually been sick, vomited, or is it just the queasy feeling?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Just queasy. I haven't vomited.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She left her breakfast sitting there. And she's asked me is it a stroke about ten times since Sunday.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're a little warm, that thirty-eight point three. Any cough, a sore throat, or burning when you pass water?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not really. I don't feel fluish, I was just rushing.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. I want to lie you back for a few seconds and watch the eyes. It's a positional test, a Dix-Hallpike. It can set the spinning off, then it settles. I'll have a hold of you. Is that ok?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I faint? Please don't let me faint. And will it damage the ear? I have so many questions, I'm sorry.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): You won't faint, and it won't damage anything. There now... I can see a little flicker in the eyes, and it's already settled. Sit up nice and slow.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh God that was awful. Is it a tumour? Do I need a scan? Tell me straight, doctor.

[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): I don't think it's a tumour. What I'm seeing fits benign positional vertigo, little crystals in the inner ear out of place. That's a working impression from your story and that test, not a scan result.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Crystals? Will they dissolve? Do I need an operation? And should I stop the amlodopine, is the tablet doing this?

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): No operation, and don't stop the amlodopine, today's pressure is grand. They don't really dissolve, we roll them back. I'll show you the Brandt-Daroff exercise, three times a day, until it eases.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times a day, both sides? What if I get sick halfway through? Can I drive in to work in the morning?

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both sides, yes, sitting on the bed. If you feel very sick, pause, sip some water, try again later. Don't drive while the spins are still coming. If you black out, the hearing drops, or an arm goes weak, you come straight back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): And thirty-eight point three, is that dangerous? What if the exercises do nothing? Will you scan me then, or just leave me?

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's a shade high, but with no cough or sore throat I'm not chasing an infection today. If the spinning hasn't settled, or something new shows up, we might organise a scan of the head. Otherwise no scan now. I'll see you back in two weeks to see how the exercises are going.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stand over her while she does them. She'll tell me she's doing it wrong, you know yourself.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Of course I'll do them. I'm still scared, but I will. Thanks.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Two weeks, and sooner if any of those warning signs show. Mind yourself going out.

spec.situation: Spinning for a few seconds when turning in bed or looking up, since last week; nausea; no hearing loss, no ear pain; doctor does a positional test and teaches the exercise.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Patient said “Not really,” not a definite absence of ringing.
bad.text: Ringing in the ears (status=absent, assertion=negative, reported_by=patient, temporality=current)

bad.reason: Transcript mentions being late with tablet sometimes, not unclear routine adherence to morning amlodipine.
bad.text: The patient is sometimes late with the morning amlodipine, so it is unclear if it is taken as prescribed. (type=adherence_uncertain, related_entities=medications[0], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Stopped bendrofluazide in March because it caused nocturia/being up half the night to the toilet.
Atorvastatin (or similar statin) was suggested by the chemist but the patient never started it, not once.
Headache was not clearly present: patient said 'No... well, sometimes, if I'm late with the tablet,' so this is equivocal/intermittent rather than a definite current symptom.
Positive examination detail from Dix-Hallpike: the induced spinning had already settled quickly when observed.
The doctor advised urgent review/ED also if the patient blacks out, in addition to hearing drop or arm weakness.
The doctor reassured that there is no scan now; head scan would only be considered if symptoms have not settled or if new symptoms appear.
Doctor documented not chasing an infection today despite temperature 38.3 because there was no cough or sore throat.
